summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would make changes to several intellectual property laws to improve the system.
It would allow Australian drug makers to seek a court order to produce generic versions of patented medicines for export to eligible developing countries.
The patent holder would be paid compensation negotiated to avoid disadvantaging them.
changes: Amends the Patents Act 1990, Trade Marks Act 1995, Designs Act 2003 and Plant Breeder's Rights Act 1994.
Creates a scheme for compulsory licences to manufacture and export generic pharmaceuticals to developing countries.
Implements Australia's commitment to the TRIPS Protocol.
summary.affected: Australian pharmaceutical manufacturers, patent holders, and developing countries that meet specified criteria.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Introduced the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2014, implementing the TRIPS protocol accepted by the Howard government in 2007 to let Australian manufacturers export generic medicines to countries facing health crises, extending the Federal Circuit Court's jurisdiction to plant breeders' rights disputes, and creating a single trans-Tasman patent examination process with New Zealand.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: Supported the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill implementing the WTO's TRIPS protocol, to which Australia has been a signatory since 2007, noting the World Health Organization estimates more than 100 countries face serious epidemics and that malaria, HIV-AIDS and tuberculosis infected an estimated 262 million people and caused 3.8 million deaths in 2011, but criticised the removal of Crown use provisions relating to gene patents.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Laming
speeches.brief: Discussed the TRIPS protocol's history in the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill, noting Vietnam's life expectancy is 20 years longer than the US had a century ago at a tenth of its GDP per capita, cited research attributing over 70 per cent of the 1962 to 1987 fall in infant mortality to technology rather than income growth, and noted 38 sub-Saharan African countries spend less on health combined than the US state of Connecticut.

speeches.speaker: Alannah MacTiernan
speeches.brief: Supported the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill's TRIPS provisions but criticised the removal of Crown use provisions, noting only about half a dozen cases of Crown use of patents have ever been invoked in Australia, two of them contested, and cited a 2004 Law Reform Commission report recommending the provisions be strengthened for gene patents instead.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Supported the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill's TRIPS provisions, citing WHO estimates of 627,000 malaria deaths, 1.6 million HIV-AIDS deaths and 1.3 million tuberculosis deaths in 2012, and said improved plant breeding had let the world feed more than double its 1961 population of 3.5 billion with only a 12 per cent increase in cultivated land.

speeches.speaker: Pat Conroy
speeches.brief: Outlined the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill's implementation of the WTO's TRIPS protocol, to which Australia has been a signatory since 2007, and welcomed provisions allowing plant breeder's rights disputes to be heard in the Federal Circuit Court.

speeches.speaker: Ken Wyatt
speeches.brief: Supported the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill, recalling the Howard government's 2007 commitment to implementing the WTO's TRIPS protocol, and argued a strong IP framework is needed to protect Australian innovators and entrepreneurs in a globalised economy.

speeches.speaker: Ken Wyatt
speeches.brief: Supported the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill implementing the TRIPS Protocol, letting Australian pharmaceutical manufacturers apply for compulsory licences to export generic medicines to developing countries, allowing plant breeder's rights owners to pursue infringement cases through the cheaper Federal Circuit Court, and creating a single trans-Tasman patent application and patent attorney registration system with New Zealand.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Supported the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill implementing the TRIPS protocol to let manufacturers export generic medicines to developing countries under compulsory licence, noting it closely mirrors Labor's lapsed 2013 bill except for the removal of provisions on Crown use of patents.

speeches.speaker: Michael Sukkar
speeches.brief: Supported the bill's intellectual-property reforms, arguing that a single Australia-New Zealand patent process would reduce duplication, the TRIPS protocol would help developing countries obtain patented medicines, and document-retention and plant-breeders' rights changes would reduce regulatory costs.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Leigh
speeches.brief: Argued that the bill would implement the TRIPS protocol by allowing compulsory licences for generic pharmaceuticals during health crises in developing countries, then questioned whether stronger patent protection might impede innovation and called for a balance that maximises total innovation.

speeches.speaker: David Coleman
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, arguing that strong intellectual-property protection encourages investment while the proposed Australia-New Zealand patent process, TRIPS licensing scheme, and Federal Circuit Court jurisdiction for plant breeders would reduce costs and preserve innovation incentives.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Scott
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, arguing that intellectual-property protections would support innovation and local jobs, while its TRIPS licensing scheme, Federal Circuit Court jurisdiction for plant breeders, single Australia-New Zealand patent process, and document-retention changes would reduce costs and red tape.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Parke
speeches.brief: Supported implementing the TRIPS protocol to enable compulsory licences for generic pharmaceutical exports, but argued that Federal Court applications were costly and that gene patents, evergreening and patent monopolies could restrict research, medicines and access to healthcare.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: Supported the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2014 but argued that omitting protections for Crown use of patents weakened public access to health innovations, citing concerns about BRCA1 testing, gene patents and the effects of patent control on research and treatment.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Reported that the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2014 would reduce regulatory costs through trans-Tasman patent arrangements, TRIPS implementation, Federal Circuit Court access and document-storage reforms, while deferring Crown use changes pending consultation and the Myriad appeal.
